newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Leftist Ortega tops rival in Nicaraguan poll.
newsitem.headline: Leftist Ortega tops rival in Nicaraguan poll.

text.p: One week before Nicaraguans vote for a new president, a poll released on Sunday said controversial left-wing candidate Daniel Ortega had moved ahead of his right-wing rival, Arnoldo Aleman.

The CINCO S.A. poll gave former President Ortega, who led Nicaragua's Marxist Sandinista government from 1979 to 1990, 36.7 percent of the vote and Arnoldo Aleman, of the right-wing Liberal Alliance, 33.9 percent of the vote, followed by a jumble of 21 lesser candidates.

Ortega's popularity has soared 6.7 percentage points since CINCO's last poll in August, while Aleman's has fallen by 4.7 percentage points, reversing Aleman's nine-point lead before Nicaragua's Oct. 20 presidential vote.

Political analyst Roberto Fonseca said that despite Ortega's 2.8 percentage point lead in the poll, the vote was too close to call since the poll showed Aleman had a better image among the 16.4 percent of undecided voters.
Fonseca told news magazine Confidencial, which released the poll, "the battle continues to be close and it's too risky to predict a final result."
When asked why they support their candidate, Ortega followers said it was because "he cares about people," while Aleman supporters said their candidate would "improve the country."

Fonseca said Ortega was seen by some as "the candidate of the poor" while Aleman was seen as "the candidate of the rich," a designation that costs him votes, as Nicaragua is one of the poorest countries in the Western hemisphere.
The majority of those polled said Ortega would be better at creating employment than Aleman.

Only four months ago Aleman seemed a sure bet as Nicaragua's next president. But since then Ortega's popularity has steadily climbed thanks to a smooth campaign that has changed his image from a fiery revolutionary into a moderate, centre-left politician willing to work with private enterprise and his old enemies.
If neither candidate receives 45 percent of the vote, a run-off election between the two top vote-getters will be held on an unspecified date in early December.

The CINCO poll surveyed 1,589 Nicaraguans between Sept. 29 and Oct. 7 with a margin of error of 2.4 percent. But pollsters did not reach the remote Atlantic autonomous regions or the southern Rio San Juan region, which together contain about 10 percent of the electorate.
